name: Centre for Long-Term Resilience (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: pandemics and an AI catastrophe kill people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population; the work is aimed at the UK government.
summary: The Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR, London) advises the UK government on extreme risks through three policy units: biosecurity (the UK's Biological Security Strategy, DNA synthesis screening, mirror life), AI (frontier AI regulation, misuse, incident response) and risk management (how government assesses and prepares for risks). This model covers all its work in its year to 30 November 2025, about $2.9M; its filed accounts leave out the income and expenditure account, so spending is built from its 19 staff and its advertised pay. At the defaults it averts about 6 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.3 to 95 on the combined range: each dollar is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risks of a pandemic and an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), with deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate; after each branch's adjustments about 85% of the result is the biosecurity work (about half the cost), a tenth the AI work and the rest risk management, and no law or standard it worked on was won in the year. The biggest uncertainties are how much a dollar of pandemic work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; ten times either way), the years a cut counts and the next-dollar figure (53%); every branch is discounted for missing data, since no outcome of the work is measured.

rows.explainer: CLTR's advertised pay: a biosecurity policy adviser £63.4k to £80k (2024, the source); an AI policy manager or senior manager £65,388 to £93,723 (https://www.jobijoba.co.uk/detail/92/19f806335e1187445bb24a89b8027ae5); a biosecurity policy manager £70,000 to £90,000 (https://findroles.com/jobs/5572536804-biosecurity-policy-manager); a strategic communications lead £80,000 to £90,000 (2026, https://smartthinking.org.uk/?p=52776); an operations associate £55,000 (https://www.charityjob.co.uk/jobs/centre-for-long-term-resilience/operations-associate/1073946). Of the 20 staff on its team page, 12 are directors, senior advisers or senior policy managers, the rest operations, delivery and fundraising staff. About £75,000 on average, our estimate from those adverts, £62,000 (operations-heavy, junior pay) to £90,000 (senior-heavy); the PAYE and NI owed at the year end (accounts note 6, £50,213, about a month's tax on 19 such salaries) agrees.

rows.label: Total expenses in the year to 30 November 2025 (all programmes, management, fundraising)
rows.explainer: Built from staff pay over its share of all spending (staff_cost_share), since the accounts leave out the income and expenditure account: about $2.9M (£2.2M). Cross-check from funders: Coefficient Giving (then Open Philanthropy) committed £4M over three years from October 2024 (about £1.33M a year) with a match of up to £3M more; the Survival and Flourishing Fund recommended $1.08M (2024) and $565,000 (2025); Sentinel Bio gave $400,000 (February 2025); and members' funds rose by £601,306 in the year (balance sheet: £272 to £601,578), so income of about £2.7M to £3M less that surplus gives about £2.1M to £2.4M, in line. Cash of £6.3M at the year end is mostly grants received ahead (other creditors £5.7M).

rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. rows.label: AI: share of the AI spending on work against misuse (open-source and misuse risks, AI-enabled biology, security incidents)
rows.explainer: Of the AI unit's five focus areas, one is misuse and open-source risk, and one of its four policy staff works on AI and biology (Richard Moulange, also a Federation of American Scientists AI-biosecurity fellow); its September 2025 report on AI security incidents covers attacks as well as failures. Frontier AI regulation, companies' risk management and government incident response aim at both and count as misalignment work, as the family's rule says; loss-of-control monitoring is misalignment. 25%, our judgment, 15% to 40%, a little above GovAI's 20%.

rows.label: AI field work: how far the typical project's effect applies to its catastrophe work
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project applies to the AI unit's work: advice to UK officials on frontier AI legislation, incident reporting and the government's response to incidents, risk management at AI companies (its three-lines model), reports and evidence to Parliament; CLTR's recommendations were taken into the Ministry of Defence's AI strategy earlier, but no uptake is measured for the year. 0.75 (0.3 to 1.2), our judgment, between the template's 0.7 for typical policy work and the Council on Strategic Risks' 0.8 for biological policy with government access.

rows.explainer: One of the AI unit's five focus areas is chronic and societal risks (AI's effects on institutions and society), which the catastrophe chances don't cover; its value is in unmodelled_benefits_adj. A little under one fifth of the unit's work: 85%, our judgment, 70% to 95%, a little above GovAI's 80% (which has a whole economics team).

rows.label: Risk management: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: Better government risk assessment, exercises and resilience structures help in a catastrophe, but they are a step further from the risk than work on the hazard itself, and much of their value is in ordinary emergencies (in unmodelled_benefits_adj). 0.4 (0.1 to 0.8), our judgment, as the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security's outbreak analytics and the Council on Strategic Risks' foresight lab, each a step removed from the catastrophic risk.

rows.explainer: Applied: each branch's own multiplier (<branch>_evidence_adj), weighted by the branches' healthy years (w_<branch>), so that evidence_adj × counterfactual_adj × attribution_share is each branch's own product weighted by its value, never by its spending. The risk management branch (rm_) added beside the template's five.

The risk management branch (rm_) added beside the template's five.
rows.formula: (w_ai * ai_evidence_adj * ai_counterfactual_adj + w_bio * bio_evidence_adj * bio_counterfactual_adj + w_nuclear * nuclear_evidence_adj * nuclear_counterfactual_adj + w_pol * pol_evidence_adj * pol_counterfactual_adj + w_fb * fb_evidence_adj * fb_counterfactual_adj + w_rm * rm_evidence_adj * rm_counterfactual_adj) / (w_total * evidence_adj)

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Coefficient Giving matches other donors' gifts £1 for £1 up to £3M (October 2024), but its matched pound would otherwise fund other work of about the same value, and whether the match is still open isn't published; whether large funders give less if small donors give more is the room factor of @next_dollar.centre_for_long_term_resilience (one question per adjustment). 1, our judgment, as every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.1.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of CLTR's work on the risks is measured (each branch is a typical project's cut and the shared forecast chances), so the shared missing-data step applies to every branch (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted, each part a share of the modelled value: the risk management work's value in ordinary emergencies (floods, cyber attacks on infrastructure, outbreaks far smaller than COVID-19) and the AI unit's work on chronic and societal risks (both left out of the chains by rm_evidence_adj and ai_catastrophe_relevant_share), about 6%; smaller AI misuse and AI incidents than a catastrophe (no shared forecast: ai_smaller_per_year 0), medicines-supply security and mentoring for others' biosecurity fellowships, about 4%. 10% (3% to 30%), our judgment, between the Council on Strategic Risks' 5% and GovAI's 15%.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut. CLTR builds no capabilities; its 2026 case for 'defensive acceleration' of the UK bioeconomy and its framing of UK leadership in AI could add a little to the pace of the technologies whose risks it works on. −1%, our judgment, 0 to −3%, as the Council on Strategic Risks' and the Johns Hopkins Center's lower end.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: its mirror-life work identifies knowledge gaps (it says without lowering the barriers to creating mirror life), its AI-biology risk index ranks dangerous biological tools, and incident analyses describe how AI systems fail; all are policy-level and reviewed. −2.5%, our judgment, 0 to −6%, a little below GovAI's −3% for published threat models because more of CLTR's work is advice to officials than published analysis.

Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Staff pay's share of all spending, from CLTR's own accounts (Convention 1), which give no salary line but two checks. Staff pay: the PAYE and National Insurance owed at the year end (£50,213, note 6) is about one month's tax on 19 salaries of about £75,000 (income tax, employee and employer NI, about £31,400 a person a year, £49,800 a month), so the staff count and pay below hold. Total spending: the year's income (Coefficient Giving's £4M over three years from October 2024, about £1.33M a year; the Survival and Flourishing Fund's $1.08M and $565,000; Sentinel Bio's $400,000; other donors) less the £601,306 surplus is about £2.1M to £2.4M, against staff pay of about £1.8M with benefits: 0.74 to 0.85. The rest is the London office, travel, events, contractors and fees. 0.8 (0.7 to 0.9). It sets total_expenses (staff pay over this share); the result per dollar doesn't depend on the cost's size, since each branch's cut grows with its spending, so the share matters only through staff's forgone pay (salary_sacrifice, with credit by share of resources on).
